series: SSDF rating list: top-rated chess program on each published list (rating as published)
unit: SSDF rating (Elo scale fitted to engine-vs-engine games at tournament time control on SSDF's reference machines; its level was set by occasional games against Swedish and Elo-rated human players)
description: The Swedish Chess Computer Association (SSDF) published a rating list of chess computers and programs from 1984 to 2023-12-31, its last list. Each point is one dated list: the top program (with the hardware it ran on) and its rating, games and margin of error as printed on that list, 1994-05-28 to 2023-12-31, 92 lists. The SSDF site keeps only its final list, so earlier lists come from SSDF's own pages as the Internet Archive captured them on each of its hosts (1998-2026), from the lists SSDF's chairman posted on the CCC forum (talkchess.com, 2007-2023), and, before 1998, from copies posted to Usenet or mirrored by Manfred Rosenboom (whose pages reword some hardware names). Where several copies of one list exist, the SSDF's own page is used and the others cross-check it ('cross_checked'). frontier = the rating is a new high for the series. median_shift_vs_previous and previous_leader_change compare each list with the previous point (see caveats). other_series: (1) the SSDF leaders of 1984-1993 from SSDF's own history page (year only); (2) every one of these leaders re-rated on SSDF's final list, one consistent scale; (3) CCRL 40/15, a separate pool and scale, 2006 to today. Never draw SSDF and CCRL as one line.
license: No open license is stated. SSDF's list page says the list 'may be quoted' provided that not only the ratings but also the number of games and the margin of error are quoted (here 'games', 'err_plus', 'err_minus'). CCRL's pages state no terms. Cite SSDF (ssdf.bosjo.net) and CCRL (computerchess.org.uk/ccrl); the 1984-1993 values are from Tony Hedlund's SSDF history page.
sources: http://ssdf.bosjo.net/long.txt (final list, 2023-12-31, every computer tested since 1984)
https://web.archive.org/ (captures of SSDF's list pages on home3.swipnet.se, w1.859.telia.com, web.telia.com and ssdf.bosjo.net; CCRL's list page)
https://www.talkchess.com/forum/ (SSDF lists posted by SSDF's chairman, 2007-2023)
https://web.archive.org/web/20000818193559id_/http://home3.swipnet.se:80/~w-36794/ssdf/comment.htm (SSDF chairman's comment on the 2000-08-04 list: the 100-point recalibration)

human_ceiling.note: The highest FIDE standard rating any player has held: Carlsen's 2882 on the FIDE lists of 2014-05 and 2019-08. FIDE ratings come from human-vs-human games; the engine lists are a different pool, so a line at this height on an engine chart is a reference, not a common scale.

engines_passed_humans.event: IBM's Deep Blue beats world champion Garry Kasparov 3.5-2.5 in a six-game match in New York (May 3-11, 1997), the first computer to beat a reigning world champion in a match under standard tournament time controls. A purpose-built IBM supercomputer: per IBM, 32 processors evaluating 200 million positions per second.
engines_passed_humans.kind: first match won against the world champion

engines_passed_humans.event: Deep Fritz beats world champion Vladimir Kramnik 4-2 in Bonn (Nov 25 - Dec 5, 2006), running on a commercially available PC. Wikipedia: chess programs on commercially available desktop computers won decisive matches in 2005 and 2006; this was the last major human-computer match, and 'since that time, chess programs running on commercial hardware ... have been able to defeat even the strongest human players.' This is the usual date for engines on ordinary hardware staying ahead of the best humans.
engines_passed_humans.kind: engines on ordinary hardware stay ahead
sources: https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Computer_chess&oldid=1378366571 (secondary: 'By 2006, programs running on desktop PCs had attained the same capability')

engines_passed_humans_context.event: Hydra (custom hardware, 64 processors) beats Michael Adams, then ranked seventh, 5.5-0.5 in a six-game match (ChessBase's report is dated June 28, 2005).
Pocket Fritz 4 (Hiarcs 13) on an HTC Touch HD phone wins the Copa Mercosur in Buenos Aires (Aug 4-14, 2009) with a performance rating of 2898.

caveats: Engine-vs-engine pools. SSDF and CCRL ratings come from games between programs and are tied to human ratings loosely or not at all. SSDF set its level from 337 tournament games against Swedish players in 1987-1991, then, finding from games between computers and Elo-rated humans (Chris Carson's compilation) that 'the level of the list is about 100 points too high', lowered the whole list by 100 points with the list of 2000-08-04 (chairman Thoralf Karlsson's comment on that list). SSDF itself says the list 'does not necessarily say which ELO-rating a certain program would achieve' against humans. CCRL states no human anchor. A 3500 on either list is not a FIDE 3500, and SSDF and CCRL are not on one scale either.

SSDF moved its whole scale several times, so as-published values jump without any program changing: per SSDF's history page the level was lowered by 49, 23, 17-22, about 3, about 18 and about 70 points between 1985 and 1989 and raised by 24 in 1990; per the chairman it was then unchanged from summer 1991 until it was lowered by 100 points on 2000-08-04 (earlier points carry a note). The lists themselves show it: median_shift_vs_previous on each point is the median change, from the previous point, of every program on both lists; moves of 15 or more: 2000-04-07 to 2000-08-04: -100 (47 programs). The re-rated series in other_series puts every leader on the final list's single scale and removes these jumps.

CCRL's scale moved too, by the same measure (median change of the engines on consecutive quarterly lists): 2012-02-29 to 2012-06-23: -96 (209 engines); 2012-06-23 to 2012-10-01: -23 (225 engines); 2012-10-01 to 2013-01-05: +21 (234 engines); 2023-12-29 to 2024-04-05: -22 (504 engines). Its top also moved apart from the median: Houdini 2.0c 64-bit 4CPU 3210 on 2012-06-23 to 3249 on 2012-10-01 (median engine -23); Stockfish 20230613 64-bit 4CPU 3540 on 2023-12-29 to 3642 on 2024-04-05 (median engine -22). Across those pairs of lists the change in CCRL's top rating is mostly the scale, not a stronger engine (the points carry a note). There is no re-rated CCRL series here because its archived pages give no final fit of old entries.

Hardware changes over time, and part of every rise is the machine. SSDF rated program and machine together: dedicated chess computers to 1993, then fixed PC levels (hardware.htm lists Pentium 90, P200 MMX, K6-2 450, Athlon 1200, the quad-core Q6600 2.4 GHz and the eight-core Ryzen 7 1800X 3.6 GHz). The top entry ran on: 486/50-66 1994; Pentium 90 1995-1997; P200 MMX 1997-1999; K6-2 450 1999-2001; Athlon 1200 2001-2007; Q6600 2008-2017; Ryzen 1800X 2017-2022; RTX 3060 Ti GPU 2021-2023 (each point's model names it). CCRL normalizes time controls to a benchmark machine (Athlon 64 3800+, then Athlon 64 X2 4600+, then an i7-4770k once 40/40 was renamed 40/15) and its top entries are mostly 4-CPU versions; see each point's time_control.

The human ceiling is on a different pool: Carlsen's 2882 is a FIDE rating from human games. The last SSDF list before Deep Blue's win (1997-04-26) was topped by Hiarcs 6.0 Pentium 90 MHz at 2465 (pre-2000 scale; 2339 on the final list), and the last before Deep Fritz beat Kramnik (2006-11-24) by Rybka 1.2 256MB Athlon 1200 MHz at 2918 (2907 on the final list). Deep Blue was special hardware far beyond the PCs SSDF tested; the crossing of the numbers in 2006 lines up with the matches only roughly.

Ratings on one list are refitted on the next as games accumulate, so the same program's rating drifts from list to list (largest move between consecutive points with the same leader, apart from the 2000 cut: Rybka 2.3.1 Arena 256MB Athlon 1200 MHz, 2962 on 2007-04-21 and 2935 on 2007-11-03). The as-published series shows each list as printed.

Coverage. 92 dated lists, every one whose text could be recovered; SSDF published more (up to eight a year in the late 1990s, two a year at the end), so the gaps are lists nobody archived. Years with one list or none here: 1995, 2008, 2011, 2012, 2021. Before 1994 no dated list survives online; the 1984-1993 leaders come from SSDF's narrative history and are dated to the year only (date_precision 'year' uses July 1 as a chart placeholder). The SSDF list ended with the 2023-12-31 list.

Selection. A point is the top of the list on that date. A new program can top a list on few games with a wide margin (err_plus, err_minus) and fall back on the next list; frontier flags any new high, including those. frontier compares as-published values, so after the 100-point cut it stays false until the top passes the pre-cut high (2721 on 2000-04-07) again, on 2001-10-02; the re-rated series' frontier has no such gap.

Wikipedia's SSDF 'Rating list year-end leaders' table, the figures usually quoted, mixes scales. Compared with the last list of each year here, where both name the same program and hardware: from 2008 its rating is the published one in 12 of 13 years; before 2000 (1996, 1997, 1998, 1999) it is a median 116 points below the published rating and 5.5 from the same entry on SSDF's final list, so those rows are later re-ratings, not what the lists printed. For 2021, 2022, 2023 it names a different program or version from the year's last list. Do not chart it against the as-published points; see wikipedia_year_end_crosscheck.

other_series.description: The final SSDF list rates every computer SSDF tested since 1984 in one fit of all 164540 games. Each point is a list leader from the main series (or the early series) with its rating on that final list, so the recalibrations of 1985-1990 and 2000 drop out. A leader's final-list rating can differ from its as-published rating by more than a recalibration because ratings are refitted as games accumulate. Names were matched across SSDF's 2018 renaming by normalized name or, for retired entries, by their unchanged game count and score.

other_series.unit: CCRL rating (Bayeselo fit of engine-vs-engine games; its own scale, not SSDF's)
other_series.description: Computer Chess Rating Lists, testing since Dec 19, 2005. The list page as the Internet Archive captured it, first capture of each calendar quarter, plus the current list. Each point: the top of the 'best versions' list on its stated date. Ratings are refitted on every update, and the time control and benchmark machine changed (time_control field). The scale itself moved: median_shift_vs_previous is the median change, from the previous point, of every engine on both lists (moves of 15 or more: 2012-02-29 to 2012-06-23: -96 (209 engines); 2012-06-23 to 2012-10-01: -23 (225 engines); 2012-10-01 to 2013-01-05: +21 (234 engines); 2023-12-29 to 2024-04-05: -22 (504 engines)), and previous_leader_change is the previous point's leader's change (apart from the median by 50 or more: Houdini 2.0c 64-bit 4CPU 3210 on 2012-06-23 to 3249 on 2012-10-01 (median engine -23); Stockfish 20230613 64-bit 4CPU 3540 on 2023-12-29 to 3642 on 2024-04-05 (median engine -22)).

wikipedia_year_end_crosscheck.note: Wikipedia's SSDF 'Rating list year-end leaders' table, the figures usually quoted, mixes scales. Compared with the last list of each year here, where both name the same program and hardware: from 2008 its rating is the published one in 12 of 13 years; before 2000 (1996, 1997, 1998, 1999) it is a median 116 points below the published rating and 5.5 from the same entry on SSDF's final list, so those rows are later re-ratings, not what the lists printed. For 2021, 2022, 2023 it names a different program or version from the year's last list. Do not chart it against the as-published points; see wikipedia_year_end_crosscheck.

trend.method: Computed by experiments/chess/build.py. year_end: the last list dated in that year. per_decade_ols: least-squares slope of rating on date over the points dated within the decade, times ten. first_above_human_ceiling: the first point rated above Carlsen's FIDE peak, a cross-pool comparison that only says when the numbers crossed. These are descriptive fits to the published tops, not a model.
